newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity up slightly despite bearishness.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity up slightly despite bearishness.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were trading slightly higher Thursday despite continued bearish fundamentals, industry sources said.
"The market has shown some strength, perhaps some people are going long and betting on more (generation) unit outages," said one New York based futures trader.

Power futures continued to show some of the strength seen Wednesday, based in part on news the the 1,221 megawatt (MW) unit 2 at the Palo Verde nuclear complex in Arizona would begin Sunday to slowly ramp down to between 60 and 80 percent power by September 6, when it was scheduled to shut for refueling.
But sources said overall fundamentals pointed towards a weaker market.
"We're looking at some cooler weather in the West, and people had been looking for the Palo Verde unit to shut down in September all along," the New York source said.

As of 1230 EDT, August Palo Verde (PV) futures were trading up 25 cents at $34.95 per megawatt hour (MWh) following exchanges in a range of $34.80-35.20, while September was up 27 cents at $28.00 following trades in a range of $27.90-28.30 per MWh.

August California Oregon Border (COB) was trading up nine cents at the day's low of $21.10 after hitting a high of $21.25, while September COB was up 40 cents at the day's high of $21.90 after reaching as low as $21.80 per MWh.
NYMEX said as of 1155 EDT an estimated total of 180 PV and 196 COB contracts had traded.

Forcasts called for temperatures in the Pacific Northwest to be coolest over the central and eastern sections over the next week, averaging three to five degrees Fahrenheit below normal, with readings one to two degrees below normal in the west.

In the Southwest, temperatures were expected to average three to five degrees below normal over most of the region through into early next week, with temperatures near normal in the extreme east, south and west sections.

In Western generation news, the 1,070 MW SONGS unit 2 at the in southern California was at 98 percent power early Thursday, while the neighboring 1,080 MW unit 3 was at 86 percent and was increasing to full power.

Separately, on Wednesday the Western Systems Coordinating Council approved a final summertime capacity for the Pacific Intertie of 6,900 megawatts (MW). The new rating will replace an interim summer cap of 6,300 MW which has been in place since July 1.
